lessons.title: Read a ticker
lessons.summary: Use a ticker to identify a market listing.
lessons.salIntro: Read the label before you read the noise.
lessons.salComplete: Good. A familiar ticker is a clue, not proof.

steps.prompt: What is a ticker?

choices.label: A short label for a market listing
A private password for the company

steps.correctFeedback: Right. A ticker is a short label used for a market listing.
steps.incorrectFeedback: A ticker is a short label used for a market listing.

steps.prompt: Which pair matches a company and its exchange ticker?
steps.correctFeedback: Yes. AAPL is Apple's exchange ticker.
steps.incorrectFeedback: AAPL is Apple's exchange ticker.

steps.prompt: What does a ticker identify most precisely?
steps.correctFeedback: Correct. A ticker points to a listing, so the market still matters.
steps.incorrectFeedback: A ticker identifies a market listing, not a company's products.

steps.prompt: AAPLx appears in a wallet. Is AAPL alone enough to verify it?

choices.label: No, check the issuer and mint

steps.correctFeedback: Exactly. A token symbol can resemble a ticker. Verify the issuer and mint.
steps.incorrectFeedback: A familiar ticker does not verify a token. Check the issuer and mint.

lessons.title: Why prices move
lessons.summary: Connect price changes to buyers, sellers and changing expectations.
lessons.salIntro: Find what changed before you chase the move.
lessons.salComplete: Good. Prices move on expectations, not headlines alone.

steps.prompt: What can move a stock price?

choices.label: Buyers and sellers changing their offers
A fixed price chosen by the company

steps.correctFeedback: Right. Trades meet where buyers and sellers agree.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Market prices respond to the offers buyers and sellers make.

steps.prompt: A company reports stronger sales than expected. Why might its price move?
steps.correctFeedback: Yes. New information can change what buyers and sellers expect.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Prices can move when new information changes expectations.

steps.prompt: Can a healthy company fall when the wider market falls?

choices.label: Yes, wider market moves can affect it

steps.correctFeedback: Correct. Sector and market moves can affect an individual stock.
steps.incorrectFeedback: A stock can move with its sector or the wider market.

steps.prompt: Does good news guarantee the next price move?

choices.label: No, the market may have expected it already
Yes, good news always makes it rise

steps.correctFeedback: Exactly. News, expectations and positioning all matter.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Good news does not guarantee a rise. Expectations may already include it.

lessons.title: Know the token
lessons.summary: Check what a tokenized stock represents and who issued it.
lessons.salIntro: Check the wrapper before you call it a stock.
lessons.salComplete: Good. You checked the product, not just the logo.

steps.prompt: How do you know what a tokenized stock represents?
steps.correctFeedback: Right. The issuer's terms define the token and its holder rights.
steps.incorrectFeedback: The issuer's terms define what the token represents.

steps.prompt: Should you assume every stock token is a share in a brokerage account?

choices.label: Yes, every token has the same rights

steps.correctFeedback: Correct. Products differ in backing, claims and holder rights.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Tokenized stock products can have different legal structures and rights.

steps.prompt: Can an on-chain stock token trade while its reference exchange is closed?

choices.label: Yes, and its price can differ

steps.correctFeedback: Yes. On-chain trading can continue while the reference market is closed.
steps.incorrectFeedback: On-chain trading can continue, and the price may differ while the reference market is closed.

steps.prompt: What should you verify before choosing a stock token?
steps.correctFeedback: Exactly. Verify the exact product, issuer and on-chain mint.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Verify the issuer, exact mint and product terms.

lessons.title: Read a red day
lessons.summary: Understand what a red move says and what it does not say.
lessons.salIntro: A red number needs a baseline.
lessons.salComplete: Good. One red day is data, not a verdict.

steps.prompt: What does a red daily move usually mean?

choices.label: The price is below its comparison point

steps.correctFeedback: Right. Red describes a price change against a chosen baseline.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Red usually means the price is below a comparison point, often the prior close.

steps.prompt: What should you check before reading a red percentage?

choices.label: The time period and comparison baseline

steps.correctFeedback: Correct. A percentage needs a starting point and time period.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Check the starting point and time period behind the percentage.

steps.prompt: Is one red day a verdict on the company?

choices.label: No, it is one data point

steps.correctFeedback: Exactly. Look at the reason, your plan and the wider context.
steps.incorrectFeedback: One red day is one data point, not a final verdict.

steps.prompt: What helps before a red day arrives?

choices.label: A position size and exit plan you can follow
A promise that the price cannot fall

steps.correctFeedback: Yes. A clear plan makes a price move easier to evaluate calmly.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Use a position size and exit plan you can follow. No price is guaranteed.

lessons.title: Trim a position
lessons.summary: Sell part of a position while keeping the rest.
lessons.salIntro: Keep some. Sell some. Know why.
lessons.salComplete: Good. A trim changes exposure without closing the position.

steps.prompt: What does trimming a position mean?
steps.correctFeedback: Right. A trim reduces a position without closing it.
steps.incorrectFeedback: A trim sells part of a position while keeping the rest.

steps.prompt: What happens to your exposure after a trim?

choices.label: It falls because you hold fewer shares

steps.correctFeedback: Correct. Holding less reduces how much that position can move your portfolio.
steps.incorrectFeedback: A trim lowers exposure because fewer shares remain.

steps.prompt: Which part of a profitable trim becomes a realized gain?
steps.correctFeedback: Yes. The sold portion realizes its gain or loss. The rest stays invested.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Only the sold portion realizes its gain or loss.

steps.prompt: Is trimming always the best decision after a gain?

choices.label: No, it depends on your plan and risk
Yes, always trim after a gain

steps.correctFeedback: Exactly. Trimming is a tool, not a rule for every position.
steps.incorrectFeedback: Trimming is one risk tool. Whether to use it depends on your plan.
